subject: security
title: Web Application Security
summary: How browsers isolate sites and how attackers get around that isolation: the same-origin policy and CORS, XSS and Content Security Policy, and CSRF with SameSite cookies.

lessons.title: Origins, sites and readable data
lessons.summary: Origins isolate reads; cross-origin requests can still reach a server.
lessons.body: You are logged into your bank in one tab and reading a dodgy blog in another. Your browser holds the bank's session cookie. If the blog's JavaScript could simply `fetch("https://bank.example/api/balance")` and read the reply, every site you visited could read every other site you were logged into. The **same-origin policy** (SOP) is the browser rule that stops this. Almost all of web security builds on it, so the rest of this module keeps coming back to it. ## What an origin is For ordinary HTTP(S) URLs, a **web origin** is the **scheme, host and port**. Two URLs are same-origin only if all three match. A default port written out (`:443` for HTTPS) counts the same as leaving it out. | URL (vs `https://shop.example`) | Same origin? | |---|---| | `https://shop.example/cart` | Yes (path ignored) | | `http://shop.example` | No: scheme | | `https://api.shop.example` | No: host | | `https://shop.example:8443` | No: port | The path, query string and fragment play no part. A subdomain is a different origin, even though it feels like "the same site". Some documents get an **opaque origin** instead, for example a sandboxed iframe that is not granted same-origin status. An opaque origin is written as `null`, but two separately created opaque origins are not the same origin, even though both print as `null`. A looser boundary, the **schemeful site**, is the scheme plus the *registrable domain* (the "eTLD+1", such as `shop.example` or `example.co.uk`). So `https://api.shop.example` and `https://www.shop.example` are **cross-origin but same-site**. Origins govern who can *read* what; sites govern when cookies are sent (the later SameSite unit). Keep the two apart. ## What the SOP actually blocks A common misconception is that the SOP stops cross-origin *requests*. Mostly it does not. It stops cross-origin *reads*. ``` evil.example page bank.example | fetch(/api/balance) | |-------------------------->| request | (cookies attached) | is SENT |<--------------------------| | response arrives, but | | JS may NOT read it | ``` The diagram assumes the page asked for credentials (`credentials: "include"`) and that the browser's cookie rules allow the cookie. A plain cross-origin `fetch` sends no cookies at all. Cross-origin interactions fall roughly into three groups: - **Writes are usually allowed.** Links, redirects and HTML form submissions can target any origin. This is why CSRF (the later CSRF units) is possible. - **Embedding is usually allowed.** ``, `

questions.prompt: Which of these URLs is **same-origin** with `https://shop.example/home`?

options.text: `http://shop.example/home`
options.explanation: The scheme differs (`http` vs `https`). Origin includes the scheme, so this is cross-origin even though host and path match.

options.text: `https://shop.example/admin?x=1`
options.explanation: Correct. Scheme, host and (default) port 443 all match. Path and query string are not part of the origin.

options.text: `https://www.shop.example/home`
options.explanation: `www.shop.example` is a different host. Subdomains are separate origins, although they are the same *site*.

options.text: `https://shop.example:8443/home`
options.explanation: An explicit port 8443 differs from the implicit 443, so the origin differs. Port is part of the triple.

questions.workedExample:
Write each URL as (scheme, host, port) and compare with (https, shop.example, 443):

| URL | Triple | Match? |
|---|---|---|
| A | http, shop.example, 80 | No |
| B | https, shop.example, 443 | Yes |
| C | https, www.shop.example, 443 | No |
| D | https, shop.example, 8443 | No |

Only B matches on all three. The path `/admin` and query `?x=1` are ignored.

lessons.title: CORS response sharing and preflight
lessons.summary: Non-safelisted CORS requests need permission before their method and headers are sent.
lessons.body:
The previous unit separated *sending* a cross-origin request from *reading* its reply. CORS is how a server lets chosen other origins read its replies.

## CORS: opting in to cross-origin reads

Modern apps legitimately need cross-origin reads. A single-page app on `https://a.test` calls an API on `https://b.test`. **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing** (CORS) lets the *server* tell the browser which other origins may read its responses.

When a page makes a CORS fetch, the browser adds an `Origin` request header saying who is asking. (Not every cross-origin navigation or embed carries one.) The server answers with headers saying what it allows:

```
GET /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example
Origin: https://a.test

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.test
Vary: Origin
```

The browser compares the allow-origin value with the page's origin:

- If it matches (or is `*` for a request without credentials), the page can read the response.
- If not, the page sees only a network error. The response did arrive; the browser just will not hand it over.
- A request sent with credentials needs more: an exact origin and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (a later unit).

## Why CORS is not access control

CORS headers are instructions to *browsers* about sharing a reply with a web page. They do not decide who may call the API:

- A simple request (below) reaches the server and runs its handler whether or not the server sends CORS headers.
- `curl`, mobile apps and attackers' servers ignore CORS entirely and read every reply.
- Restricting `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to your own front end does not stop a stolen token being used from a script.

So the server must still authenticate the caller and check what that caller is allowed to do. CORS only loosens the browser's read restriction; it never adds protection that the server lacked.

### Simple requests and preflights

Some cross-origin requests were always possible from plain HTML, for example a form POST. CORS lets those through without asking first, because holding them back would not stop anything a plain HTML form could already do. They can still change things on the server. A CORS fetch avoids a preflight when, in simplified terms:

- the method is `GET`, `HEAD` or `POST`;
- every header the page sets is on the CORS safelist, and each value meets that header's length and character rules (a safelisted name alone is not enough);
- `Content-Type`, if set, is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data` or `text/plain`.

Anything else needs permission *before* it is sent. Examples are `PUT` or `DELETE`, an `Authorization` header set by the page, or a JSON content type. Streaming request bodies and XHR upload listeners also trigger it. Unless a matching earlier approval is still cached, the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` **preflight** asking whether the real request is allowed:

```
OPTIONS /v1/orders/7 HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://a.test
Access-Control-Request-Method: DELETE
Access-Control-Request-Headers: x-token

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.test
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: x-token
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
```

If the preflight answer does not allow the method and headers, the browser never sends the real `DELETE`. If it does, the real request follows, and its response still needs its own allow-origin check before the page can read it.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: phoning ahead before an unusual delivery
> A courier delivers ordinary letters without asking. Before bringing something unusual, such as a sofa that needs a lift booked, it phones the building to check the delivery is accepted.
>
> **How it maps:** The courier is the browser, ordinary letters are simple requests, and the phone call is the `OPTIONS` preflight. The building's yes or no is the `Access-Control-Allow-*` answer; the real request goes only after a yes.
>
> **Where it stops:** The building's answer binds only this courier. Anyone delivering by another route (`curl`, a server) never phones at all. A yes also says nothing about who the sender is: it is not a login.

## Key takeaways
- CORS lets a server share responses with named origins; without it the browser hides the reply, not the request.
- Non-safelisted methods, headers or content types need a successful preflight before the real request is sent.
- CORS is not access control: non-browser clients ignore it, so the server must authenticate and authorise every request.

## Further reading
- [Fetch Standard: CORS protocol](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-cors-protocol)
- [MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS)

questions.prompt: A page on `https://evil.example` runs `fetch("https://bank.example/transfer", {method: "POST", body: "to=x"})`. The bank sends no CORS headers. Assume no CSP or other sending restriction and a reachable server. What does CORS itself do?

options.text: The browser refuses to send the request at all
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. A `POST` with a form-style body is a simple request, so it is sent without any preflight. The SOP blocks reading the response, not sending it.

options.text: The simple request can be sent, but the script cannot read the response without CORS permission
options.explanation: Correct. This simple request needs no preflight. The server may accept or reject it; absent CORS permission the response is not exposed. Default fetch credentials mode omits cross-origin cookies.

options.text: The request is sent, and the script can read the response because it was a POST
options.explanation: The method does not grant read access. Only a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header does.

options.text: The server rejects it automatically because the Origin header is foreign
options.explanation: Servers do nothing with `Origin` unless their code checks it. The SOP is enforced by the browser, not the server.

questions.workedExample: The string body gives a safelisted text/plain content type, and this POST has no unsafe author-set headers. Under the stated assumptions the browser sends it without preflight, but default cross-origin fetch does not include bank cookies. The server decides whether any action is authorised. Without allow-origin permission the CORS fetch rejects; it does not expose response contents. CSRF still matters for requests that carry eligible ambient credentials or otherwise cause an unauthorised action.

questions.prompt: A team's API at `https://api.shop.example` now sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.example`. A developer says: "Only our own front end can call the API now, so we can drop the server-side permission checks." What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Nothing: once the header is set, browsers refuse to send requests from other origins
options.explanation: This confuses reading with sending. Simple requests from any site are still sent and still run the handler; the header only decides whether the calling page may read the reply.

options.text: CORS only tells browsers which pages may read responses. Simple requests from other sites still reach the handler, and non-browser clients such as `curl` ignore CORS, so the server must still authenticate and authorise each request
options.explanation: Correct. CORS relaxes the browser's read restriction for named origins. It is not access control: anyone with a valid token can call the API from a script, and the handler runs for simple requests whatever the CORS headers say.

options.text: The header only takes effect when its value is `*`
options.explanation: A named origin is the normal (and, with credentials, the required) form. The problem is not the header's value but what the header controls.

options.text: It is fine provided the API is also served over HTTPS
options.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection from eavesdropping and tampering. It does not decide who is allowed to call the API or what they may do.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask who enforces CORS: the *browser*, on behalf of the page making the request.
2. Ask what it enforces: whether that page may **read** the response (and, for non-simple requests, whether a preflight approves sending).
3. A simple request from `evil.example` still reaches the API and runs the handler; only the reply is hidden.
4. `curl`, mobile apps and attackers' servers never apply CORS, so they can call the API directly with any token they hold.

So CORS loosens a browser restriction; it never adds server-side protection. Keep authentication and per-request authorisation on the server.

questions.prompt: A SPA makes CORS fetches to another origin, with no cached preflight permission. Assume safelisted header values where named, no extra author-set headers, no streaming body or upload-listener trigger, and no other sending restriction. Which need an OPTIONS preflight? Select all that apply.

options.text: GET /items with only Accept: application/json
options.explanation: GET with safelisted headers is a simple request; no preflight.

options.text: `POST /items` with `Content-Type: application/json`
options.explanation: Correct. `application/json` is not one of the three safelisted content types, so it needs a preflight.

options.text: `DELETE /items/3`
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied empty-cache conditions. DELETE is not a CORS-safelisted method.

options.text: `GET /me` with an `Authorization: Bearer ...` header
options.explanation: Correct. `Authorization` is not a CORS-safelisted header, so even a GET is preflighted.

options.text: `POST /upload` with `multipart/form-data`
options.explanation: `multipart/form-data` is safelisted (an HTML form can send it), so this is a simple request.

questions.workedExample: Under these assumptions, GET with a safelisted Accept value and POST with a safelisted multipart content type avoid preflight. JSON content type, DELETE and the Authorization header require permission and therefore OPTIONS with an empty preflight cache. Header lengths/bytes and API-specific flags matter too; a header name alone is not the complete safelist test.

lessons.title: Preflight cache lifetime and matching
lessons.summary: A cached permission has a bounded lifetime and specific matching conditions.
lessons.body:
The previous unit's preflight approved a cross-origin `DELETE` carrying an `x-token` header. Sending an extra `OPTIONS` before every such request costs a round trip, so the browser can remember a successful preflight and reuse it. This **preflight cache** is separate from the ordinary HTTP cache that stores page and API responses.

## How long the permission lasts

The server suggests a lifetime with `Access-Control-Max-Age`, in seconds. The browser then applies its own rules:

- **It uses whichever is shorter:** the server's request or the browser's own cap.
- **Chromium's cap is two hours** (7,200 seconds) in its current source. Other browsers use their own caps, and they can change between versions.
- **A missing or invalid value means five seconds**, the default in the Fetch Standard.
- **The browser may forget sooner.** The standard allows early removal at any time, and a CORS failure on a later request to the same URL clears the matching entries. The requested lifetime is an upper limit, not a promise.

So the earlier `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600` lets the browser skip new preflights for at most ten minutes. A server sending 86,400 (one day) still gets at most two hours in Chromium. If you see `OPTIONS` requests reappearing in your logs, that is the browser's cap or eviction at work, not a server bug.

## When a cached permission can be reused

Reuse needs a close match with the original preflight:

- **Same requester and target:** the same requesting origin, the same URL, and the same top-level site (browsers keep a separate preflight cache for each site the user is visiting).
- **Covered method and headers:** a later request with a method or header that the cached answer did not allow needs a new preflight. One that the cached answer already covers does not.
- **Credentials:** an approval obtained for a request with credentials can cover a later request without them, but not the other way round.

The cache only saves the browser from asking again. It never weakens the server's own checks, which still run on every real request.

## Key takeaways
- The browser keeps a preflight approval for the shorter of the server's requested lifetime and its own cap, and may drop it sooner.
- A missing or invalid `Access-Control-Max-Age` gives only five seconds of reuse.
- Reuse needs the same origin, URL and top-level site, plus a cached answer that covers the method, headers and credentials mode.

## Further reading
- [Fetch Standard: CORS protocol](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-cors-protocol)
- [Chromium preflight result implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chromium/chromium/main/services/network/cors/preflight_result.cc)

questions.prompt: Your API answers preflights with `Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400` (one day). Your API's logs show each Chromium user's browser still sending a new `OPTIONS` request from the same page, for the same URL, method and headers, roughly every two hours. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The header value is invalid, so the browser falls back to the 5-second default
options.explanation: A missing or invalid value does give 5 seconds, but then you would see a preflight before almost every request, not one every two hours. 86400 is a valid number of seconds.

options.text: Chromium caps the preflight cache at two hours, and the browser uses the shorter of the server's requested lifetime and its own cap
options.explanation: Correct. The server can only ask for a lifetime; the browser applies its own maximum (two hours in current Chromium source) and may drop the entry even sooner.

options.text: Browsers never cache preflights; each OPTIONS request is triggered by a new user action
options.explanation: Browsers do cache successful preflights, for up to the requested lifetime (subject to their cap). That is why the requests are two hours apart rather than before every call.

options.text: A CDN's HTTP cache is expiring the stored OPTIONS response every two hours
options.explanation: The preflight cache lives in the browser and is separate from HTTP caching. A shared CDN cache could only change how many OPTIONS requests reach your server; it cannot make each user's browser send one every two hours. That is decided by the browser's own preflight cache.

questions.workedExample:
1. The server asked for one day (86,400 seconds).
2. Fetch lets each browser impose a cap; current Chromium source caps preflight caching at two hours.
3. The browser keeps the approval for whichever is shorter, so at most two hours.
4. When it expires, the next matching request needs a new `OPTIONS`, which matches the two-hour pattern in the logs.

Asking for a longer lifetime changes nothing in Chromium. Other browsers have their own caps, and any browser may drop an entry early, so never rely on the requested lifetime as a guarantee.

lessons.title: Credentialed CORS and exact allowlists
lessons.summary: Cookie eligibility, exact allowed origins and cache variation are separate checks.
lessons.body:
This unit looks at an API that shares *user-specific* responses with a few named front-end origins. That is where CORS mistakes do the most damage, because the replies contain private data. The Python snippets are fragments of a Flask app, shown only to study the response headers; they are not complete authentication or preflight handlers.

### Credentials

By default, a cross-origin `fetch` sends no cookies. Setting `credentials: "include"` lets the browser attach cookies, but only those that its cookie rules allow (SameSite, third-party-cookie blocking and so on).

To let the page *read* a credentialed response, the server must say so explicitly:

- It must send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` must name the exact origin. The CORS wildcard `*` is **not allowed** with credentials; the browser treats the response as a CORS failure.

This rule exists so that nobody can accidentally say "any site may read this user's private data".

## The classic CORS misconfiguration

Because `*` cannot be combined with credentials, developers sometimes "fix" the error by echoing back whatever `Origin` arrives. That is a credentialed wildcard in disguise. If a victim's cookies are sent and the endpoint returns their data, any site the victim visits can read it.

Vulnerable Flask hook (assume `app` and `request` are provided; do not deploy it):

```python
@app.after_request
def cors(resp):
    o = request.headers.get("Origin")
    # BAD: grants read access to any origin
    resp.headers[
        "Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = o
    resp.headers[
        "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials"
    ] = "true"
    return resp
```

Fixed hook with an exact allowlist (same setup assumptions):

```python
ALLOWED = {
    "https://a.test",
    "https://admin.example",
}

@app.after_request
def cors(resp):
    o = request.headers.get("Origin")
    # Share only with a known app origin.
    if o in ALLOWED:
        resp.headers[
          "Access-Control-Allow-Origin"] = o
        resp.headers[
          "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials"
        ] = "true"
    # caches must key on Origin
    resp.vary.add("Origin")
    return resp
```

A request from `https://evil.example` now gets no allow-origin header, so its page cannot read the reply. The server still runs the handler, which is why the endpoint also needs its own authentication, authorisation and CSRF protection.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a door with a guest list
> A private party has a guest list at the door. A lazy doorman, asked to "only let in people on the list", instead asks each visitor their name and writes it on the list before checking it.
>
> **How it maps:** The list is the set of allowed origins and the visitor's name is the `Origin` header. Echoing `Origin` back is the lazy doorman: every visitor passes. A real allowlist compares the name with a list written in advance.
>
> **Where it stops:** Unlike a spoken name, `Origin` is set by the browser, and a web page cannot change it. (A non-browser client can send any value, but it does not carry the victim's cookies.) So the danger is not lying but *which* sites are on the list: any listed origin, even a compromised one, gets in.

## Other common mistakes

For the subdomain example below, cross-site scripting (XSS) means an attacker's script running inside a trusted page's origin; the later XSS units examine that bug.

- **Sloppy matching.** Checking `origin.endswith("example.com")` also accepts `https://evilexample.com`. A regular expression without anchors or with an unescaped `.` has the same problem. Compare complete origins exactly.
- **Trusting `null`.** Sandboxed iframes, `file:` pages and some redirects send `Origin: null`. Any website can create a sandboxed iframe, so an attacker can produce `null` on demand. Never allowlist it.
- **Trusting every subdomain.** If `*.example.com` is allowed and one forgotten subdomain has an XSS bug, the attacker reads your API through it.
- **Missing `Vary: Origin`.** When the allow-origin header depends on the request, a shared cache may store the response for one origin and serve it to another. `Vary: Origin` tells caches to keep them apart. Private per-user data also needs suitable `Cache-Control` so shared caches do not store it at all.

## Key takeaways
- `credentials: "include"` still obeys the browser's cookie rules.
- Sharing a credentialed response needs an exact named origin plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- Compare complete origins against a fixed list; echoing, suffix checks, `null` and broad subdomain trust all weaken the boundary.
- Add `Vary: Origin` when the header depends on the request, and keep private responses out of shared caches.

## Further reading
- [Fetch Standard: CORS protocol](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-cors-protocol)
- [PortSwigger original CORS research](https://portswigger.net/research/exploiting-cors-misconfigurations-for-bitcoins-and-bounties)

questions.prompt:
An API responds to a credentialed `fetch` (with `credentials: "include"`) from `https://app.example` like this:

```
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
```

What does the browser do?

options.text: Lets the script read the response, since `*` matches every origin
options.explanation: The CORS wildcard is specifically forbidden for credentialed requests. Treating `*` as "matches everything" here is the misconception.

options.text: Lets the script read the response but strips the cookies
options.explanation: Credentials mode include does not guarantee any eligible cookie exists or is sent. The CORS wildcard fails the CORS credentials-mode check regardless; stripping cookies from an already received response is not the rule.

options.text: Blocks the response: with credentials, the origin must be named exactly
options.explanation: Correct. Browsers reject `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on credentialed requests, so the fetch fails with a CORS error.

options.text: Sends a second preflight asking for the exact origin
options.explanation: There's no automatic retry. The request simply fails, and the developer must fix the server's headers.

questions.workedExample: With credentials mode include, the CORS check cannot use wildcard allow-origin, even when no cookie is eligible. An allowed named origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required to expose the response. Eligible cookies remain subject to SameSite and browser policy. For dynamically selected origins preserve Vary: Origin, and separately prevent shared caching of private user data.

questions.prompt:
An API reflects origins for which the Python suffix check below succeeds, and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Assume the attacker controls the origin being checked and eligible victim credentials are sent. Which untrusted domain passes?

```python
# A suffix does not prove ownership.
def allowed(origin):
    return origin.endswith(
        "example.com")
```

options.text: `https://example.com.evil.net`
options.explanation: This ends in `evil.net`, not `example.com`, so `endswith` returns False. (A `startswith` or `in` check would fall for it.)

options.text: `https://evilexample.com`
options.explanation: Correct. The suffix comparison accepts that string although its hostname is not example.com or its subdomain. The question assumes attacker control; whether such a domain can actually be registered is irrelevant.

options.text: None: `endswith` is a safe suffix check
options.explanation: A suffix check without a leading dot accepts any domain whose name merely ends in those letters.

options.text: `null`
options.explanation: The string `"null"` does not end in `example.com`, so this check rejects it, though an allowlist that included `null` would be a separate bug.

questions.workedExample:
Evaluate `endswith("example.com")` on each:

```
https://evilexample.com     True
https://example.com.evil.net False
null                        False
```

The fix is an exact set lookup:

```python
# Membership compares complete origins.
ALLOWED = {"https://example.com",
           "https://app.example.com"}
ok = origin in ALLOWED
```

Even `endswith(".example.com")` would trust every subdomain, including forgotten ones with XSS bugs.

questions.prompt: Your API correctly reflects allowlisted origins in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` but omits `Vary: Origin`. A CDN caches responses. What can go wrong?

options.text: Nothing, because CORS headers are evaluated by the browser, not the CDN
options.explanation: The browser evaluates them, but the CDN decides which stored copy (with which header) to hand back. That is the problem.

options.text: The cache may serve origin A's allow-origin header for origin B, causing B's CORS check to fail
options.explanation: Correct if the shared cache does not otherwise vary on Origin. Its key may include other dimensions; omission does not imply URL-only caching.

options.text: Preflights stop working because OPTIONS cannot be cached
options.explanation: Preflight caching is done by the browser via `Access-Control-Max-Age`; `Vary` is about shared caches storing the main response.

options.text: The browser will refuse every response because `Vary` is mandatory in CORS
options.explanation: Browsers don't require `Vary`. It is a correctness requirement for caches, not a browser check.

questions.workedExample: A cache stores a response authorising app.example and reuses it for admin.example because Origin is not distinguished. Admin’s browser rejects the mismatched header. Vary: Origin enables correct variation in conforming caches when the response depends on Origin; preserve other Vary values too. It does not fix unsafe shared caching of user-specific content: use appropriate Cache-Control and authentication-aware cache policy. Correctly allowlisting origins plus missing Vary does not by itself authorise an untrusted origin.

questions.prompt: An internal API allowlists `Origin: null` "so that local HTML files used by the support team work". Why is this dangerous?

options.text: It isn't: only `file:` pages can send `Origin: null`
options.explanation: Sandboxed iframes and some redirect chains also produce `null`, and any website can create a sandboxed iframe.

options.text: An attacker's page can embed a sandboxed iframe whose requests carry `Origin: null`, so the allowlist effectively trusts any website
options.explanation: Correct as a trust-boundary flaw: distinct opaque origins serialize as null. Exposing data that needs a login additionally requires eligible credentials, suitable CORS credentials permission and a sensitive response.

options.text: `null` disables the preflight, so the attacker can send DELETE requests
options.explanation: The origin value doesn't change which requests are preflighted; that depends on method and headers.

options.text: Browsers convert `null` to `*`, which breaks credentials
options.explanation: Browsers do not rewrite the value. The danger is that the allowlist matches when it shouldn't, not a conversion.

questions.workedExample: A sandboxed iframe with allow-scripts but without allow-same-origin can execute with an opaque origin serialized as null. This gives an attacker a matching origin value if the API allowlists null. Reading private data additionally depends on credential eligibility, request mode and endpoint behaviour. Do not use null as the identity of a trusted support tool; serve it from a controlled named origin.

questions.prompt: A team allows `https://*.example.com` (any subdomain) with credentials on their account API. A pen-tester reports a reflected XSS on the forgotten `https://old-promo.example.com`. Assume a logged-in victim triggers the XSS, eligible API cookies are sent, and the API responds with sensitive data. What becomes possible?

options.text: Limited to the promo site, since XSS is confined to its own origin
options.explanation: The XSS is in the promo origin, but the API has granted that origin credentialed read access, so the impact spreads to the API.

options.text: An attacker can run script on the promo origin, call the account API with the victim's cookies and read the responses
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied conditions. Trusting the compromised origin grants access to the API responses that its credentials and authorisation permit, not automatically every resource.

lessons.title: Script trust with a strict CSP
lessons.summary: A nonce policy and strict-dynamic constrain script execution without repairing unsafe output.
lessons.body:
A missed output-encoding step can survive review. **Content Security Policy** (CSP) adds a second line of defence: a response header telling the browser which scripts it may run, so that a missed bug is much harder to exploit. Encoding is the cure; CSP is the seatbelt.

## Allowlists versus nonces

An old-style **allowlist** policy names trusted hosts:

```
script-src 'self' cdn.example.com
```

The weakness is that it trusts *everything* on those hosts. If an allowed host serves a JSONP endpoint or an old library with script gadgets, an attacker who can inject HTML loads that file and steers it into running their code. Google's 2016 study of about 26,000 distinct real-world policies found that 14 of the 15 hosts most often allowlisted for scripts served such unsafe endpoints, and that about three-quarters of the policies could be bypassed through their allowlists. Those figures are a historical snapshot, but the mechanism still applies to any host allowlist.

The recommended alternative is a **strict CSP** built on nonces (a hash-based strict policy is the other option). The policy value below is wrapped for display; in the real `Content-Security-Policy` header it is one line:

```
script-src 'nonce-r4nd0mB64'
  'strict-dynamic';
object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'
```

How it works:

1. On every response, the server generates a fresh, unguessable **nonce** (at least 128 bits from a CSPRNG).
2. Each legitimate script tag carries it: `<script nonce="r4nd0mB64">`.
3. The browser runs a script element, inline or external, only if its nonce matches. Injected `<script>` tags without the nonce, inline event handlers such as `onclick`, and `javascript:` URLs are all blocked.
4. `'strict-dynamic'` passes trust on: a trusted script may create further script elements with `document.createElement` and they run without a nonce. This keeps script loaders working. In supporting browsers it also makes the policy ignore host allowlists. It does not allow `eval` or string timers, which CSP controls separately.
5. `object-src 'none'` blocks browser plugins; `base-uri 'none'` stops an injected `<base>` tag re-pointing relative script URLs.

Limits remain. If a trusted script builds a script URL or script text from attacker-controlled data, `strict-dynamic` lets that through; audit loaders for this. A nonce that leaks to the attacker, or trusted-code gadgets, can also defeat the policy.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: tonight's wristband versus a company guest list
> One venue admits "anyone from Acme Ltd or Bolt Ltd". Another stamps a different coloured wristband on invited guests each night, and staff admit only that night's colour. A guest with a wristband may bring a friend in personally.
>
> **How it maps:** The company list is an allowlist CSP: anyone from an allowed host gets in, including someone that host lets through by mistake (JSONP, gadgets). The nightly wristband is a per-response nonce, and the guest bringing a friend is `strict-dynamic` trusting scripts created by an already-trusted script.
>
> **Where it stops:** Staff check only the wristband, not the person's behaviour. A nonce proves the server placed the script, not that the script is harmless, and a trusted script that "brings in" attacker-chosen code passes too.

## Setting it in Flask

```python
import secrets
# Fragment: app and g are Flask objects.

@app.after_request
def csp(resp):
    # Match this response’s script nonces.
    n = g.csp_nonce  # set per request
    resp.headers[
      "Content-Security-Policy"] = (
        f"script-src 'nonce-{n}' "
        "'strict-dynamic'; "
        "object-src 'none'; "
        "base-uri 'none'")
    return resp

@app.before_request
def make_nonce():
    # New random bytes for this response.
    g.csp_nonce = secrets.token_urlsafe(16)
```

The template must put the same value in each intended script element. The `r4nd0mB64` string above is only a placeholder; this code generates 16 fresh random bytes per request. The next unit looks at that size and at what happens when a nonce repeats.

## Key takeaways
- CSP is an extra execution boundary; context-aware encoding is still required.
- Host allowlists trust everything an allowed host serves; a nonce trusts only scripts this response marked.
- `strict-dynamic` extends trust to scripts created by trusted scripts, so loaders must not take script URLs or text from attackers.

## Further reading
- [Content Security Policy Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/)
- [Google: strict CSP](https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp)

lessons.title: Nonce randomness, text length and reuse
lessons.summary: Random bytes establish nonce unpredictability; Base64 text length adds no entropy.
lessons.body:
The previous unit generated each CSP nonce with `secrets.token_urlsafe(16)` and put it in the policy and the script tags. A nonce works only while the attacker cannot know it, so two things matter: how hard it is to guess, and whether it is ever reused.

## How big is big enough?

CSP Level 3 says a nonce should contain at least 128 bits of randomness, counted *before* encoding, from a cryptographically secure generator. `token_urlsafe(16)` draws 16 random bytes, which is exactly 128 bits. There are so many possible values that a blind guess has no realistic chance of success.

Those bytes are then written as text in **URL-safe Base64**, which uses 4 characters for every 3 bytes and drops the `=` padding. So the nonce appears as a 22-character string.

```formula reference
b = 8n_bytes
n_chars = ⌈(4n_bytes) / 3⌉
where
b: the nonce's randomness in bits; one bit is a single random 0 or 1
n_bytes: how many random bytes the generator produces; 16 for token_urlsafe(16)
8: the number of bits in one byte
n_chars: how many characters the Base64 text has, without padding
4 / 3: Base64 writes 4 characters for every 3 bytes, because each character carries 6 bits
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number, because a part-used character still has to be written
In words: 16 random bytes give 128 bits of randomness and are written as 22 Base64 characters; the longer text adds no extra randomness.
```

The randomness comes from the bytes, not from the length of the text. A 22-character nonce built from a predictable value (a timestamp, a counter) would be worthless, however long it looks. The earlier `r4nd0mB64` was only a 9-character placeholder.

## Reuse is the real danger

Guessing is not how nonces usually fail. Reuse is:

> [!warning] Common CSP mistakes
> - A **static nonce** reused on every response is just a password printed on the page. An attacker reads it from any page and puts it on their injected script tag. Generate a new one per response.
> - **Caching** a page together with its nonce header serves the same pair to many users, so the nonce becomes reusable across those responses. Either generate fresh headers and HTML per response, or use a hash-based CSP for static pages.
> - Adding `'unsafe-inline'` without an effective nonce or hash weakens inline-script protection. `'unsafe-eval'` separately allows string-to-code execution. Neither switches off the rest of the policy.

Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first. The browser does not enforce a report-only policy; it only reports what it *would* have blocked (if reporting is configured), so you can find legitimate inline scripts before you switch to enforcement.

## Key takeaways
- A nonce needs at least 128 random bits; 16 random bytes provide exactly that.
- URL-safe Base64 writes those bytes as 22 characters without adding randomness.
- Never let a nonce repeat, whether fixed in code or frozen in a cached page; report-only mode does not block anything.

## Further reading
- [Content Security Policy Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/)
- [Python secrets](https://docs.python.org/3/library/secrets.html)
- [RFC 4648: Base64](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648)

lessons.title: Trusted Types and XSS blast radius
lessons.summary: Audit Trusted Types policies and retain protection beyond direct cookie readability.
lessons.body:
Output encoding, sanitisation and CSP each cover part of the XSS problem. This unit adds a browser feature aimed at DOM XSS, then looks at ways to limit the damage when XSS happens anyway.

## Trusted Types

DOM XSS happens when some line of client code passes an attacker-influenced string to a sink such as `innerHTML`. In a large app there can be hundreds of such lines, and reviewing each one is hard.

**Trusted Types** turns that around. With the CSP directive `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, a supporting browser refuses plain strings at covered sinks: HTML insertion such as `innerHTML`, script text, and script URLs. Those sinks then accept only typed objects, such as `TrustedHTML`, which can be created only by a named **policy**: a small function, usually wrapping a sanitiser such as DOMPurify.

- **Without a default policy**, assigning a plain string to a covered sink throws a `TypeError`.
- **With a default policy**, the browser passes plain strings through that policy instead, so its code decides what happens.
- **Review moves to the policies.** A `TrustedHTML` value is only as safe as the policy that made it, so restrict which policy names may be created (the `trusted-types` directive) and audit those policies and their callers. A sanitiser library may need its own named policy allowed deliberately.

Trusted Types does not sanitise anything by itself; it forces every risky value through code you chose. MDN lists it as supported across current major browsers since February 2026 (it shipped in Chromium-based browsers in 2020). Older browsers ignore the directive, so it must not be your only defence.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: cheques need a countersignature
> A bank teller who will pay any handwritten note is easy to fool. A teller who pays only cheques stamped by the firm's finance desk forces every payment through one checkpoint.
>
> **How it maps:** The teller is a DOM sink, the handwritten note is a plain string, and the stamp is a `TrustedHTML` object that only a policy (the finance desk) can issue. Reviewers can then audit the desk rather than every teller.
>
> **Where it stops:** The stamp is only as good as the desk's checks: a policy that returns its input unchanged stamps anything. And a default policy is like a desk that stamps every note automatically, so its checks must be strict.

## Limiting the blast radius

- **HttpOnly cookies** stop script reading the session cookie. Useful, but the attacker's script can still send requests *as* the user from inside the page, with the cookie attached automatically, and read the replies. XSS remains critical.
- **Separate origins** for user-uploaded content (Google uses `googleusercontent.com`) mean script in an uploaded file runs in a throwaway origin with nothing to steal.
- The old `X-XSS-Protection` header is obsolete; modern browsers removed the filter it controlled. Don't rely on it.

## Key takeaways
- Enforced Trusted Types rejects plain strings at covered sinks unless a default policy converts them.
- A `TrustedHTML` value is only as safe as its policy; restrict and audit policy creation.
- HttpOnly hides a cookie from script but does not stop injected script acting as the user.
- Host untrusted uploads on a separate origin, and do not rely on obsolete XSS filters.

## Further reading
- [Trusted Types specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/trusted-types/)
- [MDN: Trusted Types API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Trusted_Types_API)

lessons.title: Cookies do not establish request intent
lessons.summary: Classic CSRF depends on eligible ambient credentials and an accepted attacker-triggered action.
lessons.body:
CORS and the SOP control what a page can *read*, and XSS runs code inside an origin. **Cross-site request forgery** (CSRF) exploits a different mistake: treating a credential that the browser attaches automatically as proof that the user meant to act. The SOP stops a hostile page reading another origin's responses, but it does not stop ordinary cross-origin form submissions. The attacker can't see your bank's replies, but they don't need to. They only need the bank to *act* on a request. ## The attack You are logged in to `bank.example`, which uses a session cookie. You visit `evil.example`, which contains a hidden form: ```
``` The browser submits the form to the bank. If the browser's cookie rules (SameSite and others, covered later) allow it, the session cookie goes with it. If the endpoint accepts these predictable fields with no CSRF check or extra confirmation, it performs the transfer. ``` evil.example browser bank | form | | |------------>| | | | POST /transfer | | | Cookie: sid=.. | | |--------------->| | | 200 OK | | |<---------------| money moves ``` The root cause: **possession of the session cookie does not establish user intent**. A server that relies on the cookie alone cannot tell this request from a real one. > [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a franking machine in the post room > An office's post room stamps every outgoing letter with the company's franking mark, automatically. The bank accepts any letter carrying that mark as a genuine company instruction. A visitor slips a fake "please pay £500" letter into the outgoing tray; it gets franked like the rest. > > **How it maps:** The franking mark is the session cookie, which the browser attaches to every eligible request. The fake letter is the attacker's form. The bank checks the mark, not who wrote the letter. > > **Where it stops:** The visitor never sees the bank's reply, matching CSRF's blindness. Real post rooms don't vary their stamping by who wrote a letter, whereas browsers can withhold cookies on cross-site requests (SameSite). The fix in both cases is a check the faker cannot copy, such as a reference number known only to genuine letters: the CSRF token of the next unit. ### What CSRF can and cannot do - It can trigger any action the victim is allowed to take, as long as the attacker can predict the parameters and the endpoint has no effective CSRF check or extra confirmation. - Classic CSRF is a **blind attack**: the SOP stops the attacker reading the response. A separate CORS flaw, XSS or information leak would change that. - It rides on **ambient credentials**: cookies (or similar, such as HTTP authentication) that the browser sends automatically. An API that accepts only a bearer token added by its own JavaScript, with no ambient alternative, is not exposed to classic CSRF. - **Client-side CSRF** is a different route: input the attacker controls (for example in the URL) tricks the legitimate app's own JavaScript into sending an authenticated request. Bearer tokens do not prevent that. > [!example] Login CSRF > A twist: the attacker logs the victim into the *attacker's* account. The victim then saves a card or searches for something, and the attacker later sees it in their own account history. No logged-in victim is needed, so login forms need CSRF protection too. ## Rule zero: GET must be safe HTTP defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as **safe methods**: a request with them must not ask the server to change state for the user. (Incidental effects such as logging are fine.) If `GET /transfer?to=attacker&amount=500` moves money, a link the victim clicks, or a redirect, is enough. SameSite Lax won't help, because Lax still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations (a later unit). Where cookies are sent on subresource requests, even an `` tag can trigger it. Use POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE for state changes, with CSRF protection. ## Key takeaways - The SOP can hide a response while an accepted request still changes state. - A session cookie proves who the browser belongs to, not what the user intended. - Keep GET safe, and protect login as well as authenticated actions. - Bearer-only APIs avoid classic ambient-cookie CSRF, but client-side CSRF is a separate hazard. ## Further reading - [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) - [HTTP semantics: safe methods](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-safe-methods)

options.text: Because the attacker has stolen the user's session cookie
options.explanation: CSRF doesn't need the cookie value. The browser attaches it by itself; the attacker never sees it.

options.text: The browser attaches an eligible session cookie to the cross-site form submission, and SOP does not prevent that submission

options.text: Because the bank's CORS policy allows `evil.example`
options.explanation: CORS controls reading responses. A form POST is a simple request that goes out without any CORS permission.

options.text: Because the bank's site has an XSS vulnerability
options.explanation: XSS is a different bug (script in the bank's origin). CSRF works from the attacker's own site with no bug in the bank's HTML.

2. `evil.example` serves an auto-submitting form targeting `bank.example/transfer`.
3. Form submissions to other origins are allowed (they're writes).
4. With all applicable cookie policies permitting it, the browser includes `Cookie: sid=...`.
5. The bank sees an authenticated, valid request and acts.

The attacker never reads anything, which is why CSRF is called blind.

questions.prompt: An app deletes a user's account with `GET /account/delete`. Why is this especially bad for CSRF?

options.text: A single click on an attacker's link (or a redirect) triggers it, because `SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies on top-level GET navigations
options.explanation: Correct. GET is supposed to be safe; making it state-changing means ordinary links and redirects trigger it, and Lax cookies are sent on those. With `SameSite=None`, an image can also trigger the GET when all other cookie policies permit attachment.

options.text: GET requests are always sent without cookies
options.explanation: GETs carry cookies like any other request (subject to SameSite). That's why this is dangerous.

options.text: GET requests can't carry CSRF tokens
options.explanation: Tokens can appear in query strings but risk exposure in logs and, depending on referrer policy, Referer headers. Use an unsafe method for the operation and retain CSRF protection.

options.text: GET is fine as long as the response is JSON

Browsers issue GET requests everywhere: images, prefetches, links, previews. 3. `` cross-site is a subresource, so `Lax` cookies aren't sent; but a link click or redirect continuing a top-level navigation remains top-level, and `Lax` *does* send cookies then. 4. questions.prompt: An SPA's API accepts only a bearer token in the Authorization header, held in JS memory, with no alternative ambient authentication. Assume no XSS, token leak or client-side confused-deputy behavior. Can a hostile site's direct cross-site request perform classic authenticated CSRF?

options.text: Yes: any API that changes state needs a CSRF token

options.text: No: the browser never adds the bearer token automatically, so a faked cross-site request arrives unauthenticated
options.explanation: Correct. The attacker's page can't read the token (different origin) and the browser won't attach it, so faked requests fail authentication.

options.text: No, but only because the API uses JSON
options.explanation: JSON alone doesn't protect a cookie-based API (text/plain tricks). Here the reason is the non-ambient credential.

options.text: Yes, if the user has another tab open on the SPA
options.explanation: Other tabs don't share the in-memory token with the attacker's page; the SOP prevents that.

lessons.title: Session-bound CSRF tokens and cookie injection
lessons.summary: Reject missing tokens and bind double-submit validation to the authenticated session.
lessons.body:
The previous unit showed that a session cookie alone proves no user intent. The classic fix adds a second value that the browser does *not* attach automatically and that a hostile site cannot read: an anti-CSRF token. The Flask hooks below are illustrations; in production, use your framework's maintained CSRF protection.

## Defence 1: anti-CSRF tokens

The **synchroniser token** pattern gives the legitimate page a secret that the attacker's page can't know:

1. The server generates a random token (from a CSPRNG, at least 128 bits) and stores it in the user's session.
2. Every legitimate state-changing form or JavaScript request includes it, in a hidden field or a custom header. Never send it to other sites.
3. On every state-changing request, the server checks that the submitted token matches the session's copy, and rejects the request if it is missing or wrong.

The attacker can make the browser send the cookie, but cannot read your page to learn the token (the SOP blocks that read), so their fake request fails.

Vulnerable:

```python
# BAD: login does not establish intent.
@app.post("/transfer")
@login_required
def transfer():
    do_transfer(current_user,
                request.form["to"],
                request.form["amount"])
    return "ok"
```

Illustrative hook (assumes `app`, `session`, `request` and `abort` are set up). Render `csrf_token()` into protected forms, and issue a new session and token when the user logs in. Note that Flask's default session is a signed cookie stored in the browser, not a server-side session store.

```python
import hmac, secrets

def csrf_token():
    # Retain a token for this session.
    if "csrf" not in session:
        session["csrf"] = \
            secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    return session["csrf"]

@app.before_request
def check_csrf():
    if request.method in (
            "GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
        return
    # Prefer the form token, else a header.
    sent = (request.form.get("csrf")
        or request.headers.get(
            "X-CSRF-Token", ""))
    want = session.get("csrf")
    # no token in session: reject too,
    # or "" == "" would pass
    if (not isinstance(want, str)
            or not want
            or not want.isascii()
            or not sent.isascii()):
        abort(403)
    # ASCII, non-empty expected token above.
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sent, want):
        abort(403)
```

Three details matter here:

- **Missing must mean reject.** If both the session and the request lack a token and the code defaults both to `""`, an empty-equals-empty comparison would pass.
- **`hmac.compare_digest`** compares without stopping at the first different character, so response timing does not reveal how much of a guess was right. It accepts only ASCII strings, so the hook rejects other input instead of crashing.
- **Size:** `token_urlsafe(32)` draws 32 random bytes, which is 256 bits, double the usual 128-bit minimum. Guessing is hopeless; practical attacks instead steal or *plant* a token, which a longer token does nothing to stop.

Frameworks usually do all of this for you: Django's generated projects enable `CsrfViewMiddleware`, and Spring Security enables CSRF protection for unsafe methods by default. Check that yours is switched on and configured.

## Double-submit cookies

If you can't keep server-side session state, the **double-submit** pattern puts the token in a cookie *and* in the request body or a header, and checks they match. The attacker can't read the cookie to copy it into their form.

The naive version has a weakness: an attacker who can *write* cookies for your domain can choose both values. That includes anyone controlling a sibling subdomain, or a network attacker injecting cookies over plain HTTP. OWASP therefore recommends the **signed double-submit** variant: the token combines a random value with session-specific data under an HMAC keyed with a server secret, and the server checks the HMAC against the *current* session. A token minted for another session (such as the attacker's own) then fails.

Two more layers help against planting:

- A cookie named with the `__Host-` prefix must be `Secure`, have `Path=/` and have no `Domain` attribute. Supporting browsers then refuse to let a sibling subdomain set it. (It does not separate different ports on the same host.)
- HTTPS everywhere, with HSTS, stops network attackers injecting cookies over plain HTTP.

## Key takeaways
- Every state-changing request needs an independently checked token; reject a missing or empty one before comparing.
- Token length defeats guessing, not theft or planting.
- Bind a double-submit token to the session with an HMAC; equality of two attacker-chosen values proves nothing.
- `__Host-` cookies and HTTPS with HSTS reduce cookie injection, without replacing token validation.

## Further reading
- [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [Python hmac.compare_digest](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html#hmac.compare_digest)
- [Flask sessions](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/#sessions)

questions.prompt:
Trace this CSRF check when the session has **no** `csrf` key yet and the attacker's form sends no token:

```python
# BAD: two absent tokens compare equal.
sent = request.form.get("csrf", "")
if not hmac.compare_digest(
        sent,
        session.get("csrf", "")):
    abort(403)
```

options.text: 403: a missing token is always rejected
options.explanation: Trace it: both sides default to the empty string, and `compare_digest("", "")` is True, so `abort` is never reached.

options.text: The request passes: both values are `""`, which compare equal
options.explanation: Correct. Defaults on both sides collapse to the same value. The check must reject when the expected token is missing.

options.text: `compare_digest` raises a TypeError on empty strings
options.explanation: It accepts empty strings fine and returns True when both are empty.

options.text: The request passes only if the user is logged in
options.explanation: This snippet has no login check at all; the result is the same either way.

questions.workedExample:
Both missing values default to the empty string; compare_digest("", "") is True, so the vulnerable check passes. Reject missing expected values and non-ASCII strings before comparison:

```python
# Reject missing or malformed tokens.
want = session.get("csrf")
if (not isinstance(want, str)
        or not want
        or not want.isascii()
        or not sent.isascii()):
    abort(403)
if not hmac.compare_digest(sent, want):
    abort(403)
```

Here sent is the form string from the question. The ASCII guard also prevents a TypeError on hostile Unicode input.

questions.prompt: A naive double-submit scheme checks equality between a cookie and a submitted value. Its normal JS client reads the cookie into a header; the server also accepts the value in a form field. Which changes strengthen it against cookie injection or network attackers? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authenticate a random token together with session-specific binding data using an HMAC with a server secret, and verify it
options.explanation: Correct. A session-bound signed double-submit token prevents an attacker choosing a valid value for another session.

options.text: Name the cookie with the `__Host-` prefix
options.explanation: Correct. `__Host-` cookies must be `Secure`, have `Path=/` and no `Domain`, so a sibling subdomain can't set or overwrite them.

options.text: Make the CSRF cookie `HttpOnly`
options.explanation: The app's own JS needs to read the cookie to copy it into the header, so `HttpOnly` breaks the pattern. And it doesn't stop cookie *injection*.

options.text: Serve the whole site over HTTPS with HSTS
options.explanation: Correct. HTTPS prevents HTTP response injection on protected connections. HSTS helps when its policy is already known or preloaded; an unprotected first visit and uncovered subdomains remain deployment concerns.

options.text: Make the token longer (256 bits instead of 128)
options.explanation: The weakness is the attacker *setting* both values, not working them out. Length doesn't help.

questions.workedExample: Cookie injection alone does not let a hostile page set a custom request header through restrictive CORS. Here the server additionally accepts a form token, letting an attacker submit the planted value. Bind the signed double-submit token to the authenticated session and random nonce. A browser-enforced __Host- prefix prevents sibling-domain injection of that named cookie. HTTPS plus known/preloaded HSTS addresses network injection, subject to which hosts it covers. HttpOnly would break the stated JS cookie-reading client; making an already-unpredictable token longer does not address injection.

lessons.title: SameSite cookies and browser default modes
lessons.summary: Explicit cookie settings and request context determine cross-site sending.
lessons.body:
Tokens make the server check intent. The `SameSite` cookie attribute attacks CSRF from the other side: it lets the browser *withhold* the cookie from cross-site requests, so a faked request arrives looking logged out.

## Defence 2: SameSite cookies

Recall from the origin unit that a *site* is the scheme plus the registrable domain. So `https://app.example.com` and `https://api.example.com` are same-site, even though they are different origins. SameSite only restricts **cross-site** requests.

Here is a `Set-Cookie` value, wrapped for display (it is one line in the real header):

```http
sid=abc; Secure; HttpOnly;
SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

| Value | Cross-site requests that get the cookie |
|---|---|
| `Strict` | None at all |
| `Lax` | Top-level navigations with safe methods (clicking a link, a GET redirect) |
| `None` | SameSite imposes no restriction; other cookie policies still apply, and `Secure` is required |

So with `Lax`, the hidden-form POST from `evil.example` arrives **without** the session cookie, and the user appears logged out. `Strict` is tighter but has a usability cost: a user who follows a link from their webmail to your site arrives logged out, because that first navigation is cross-site. A common pattern is a `Lax` session cookie plus a separate `Strict` cookie that sensitive actions require.

### Browser defaults

The cookie standard's revision ("6265bis", approved but still waiting in the RFC Editor queue in October 2026) treats a cookie with no `SameSite` attribute much like `Lax`. Browsers differ. As of November 2026, both MDN's compatibility data and OWASP report that Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers have done this since 2020, Firefox only behind a non-default setting, and Safari not at all.

Chromium also adds a compatibility exception, which the draft standard permits. A cookie with **no** SameSite attribute that is at most **two minutes old** is still sent on top-level cross-site POSTs ("Lax+POST"). It exists so that some single sign-on flows keep working, and Chromium describes it as temporary. Explicitly setting `SameSite=Lax` removes it.

So **set `SameSite` explicitly** rather than relying on any browser's default:

```python
# Set transport, script and site rules.
app.config.update(
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax",
)
```

### Why SameSite alone isn't enough

- **Same-site attackers.** A compromised or taken-over subdomain (`old-blog.example.com`) is same-site with your app, so its requests carry your SameSite cookies.
- **State-changing GETs.** `Lax` sends cookies on top-level GET navigations, so a GET that transfers money is still exploitable.
- **Client-side CSRF.** Requests sent by your own JavaScript are same-site, so SameSite does nothing when attacker input steers that code.
- **Old or unusual clients** may not honour the attribute.

OWASP treats SameSite as a defence-in-depth layer to combine with tokens (or Fetch Metadata checks, next unit) in most deployments. It allows SameSite alone only in narrow cases: no untrusted hosts on the same registrable domain, no state-changing GETs, Strict (or carefully audited Lax with `__Host-`) cookies, and origin checks as an extra layer.

## Key takeaways
- Strict withholds cookies on all cross-site requests; Lax still sends them on top-level safe navigations.
- None needs Secure and is still subject to other cookie policy.
- A missing SameSite attribute is not the same as explicit Lax: defaults vary by browser, and Chromium's Lax+POST exception applies only to missing ones.
- SameSite does not stop same-site sibling attackers, client-side CSRF or state-changing GETs, so keep a CSRF token or equivalent check.

## Further reading
- [Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism (6265bis draft)](https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html)
- [Chromium SameSite guidance](https://www.chromium.org/updates/same-site/)
- [OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.prompt: A user follows a top-level link from a cross-site HTTPS webmail page to https://shop.example/orders. Authentication relies solely on a SameSite=Strict session cookie. What happens on that initial request?

options.text: The cookie is sent, because clicking a link is a user action
options.explanation: That's `Lax` behaviour. `Strict` withholds the cookie on *every* cross-site request, including top-level link clicks.

options.text: The browser blocks the navigation
options.explanation: SameSite never blocks requests; it only controls whether the cookie is attached.

options.text: The request arrives without the cookie, so the user appears logged out on landing
options.explanation: Correct. The initial cross-site navigation omits the Strict cookie. Do not assume that a browser reload necessarily changes whether SameSite treats it as cross-site.

options.text: The cookie is sent only if the link uses HTTPS
options.explanation: `Secure` controls HTTPS-only sending; `SameSite` is about the request's initiating site.

questions.workedExample:
1. Initiator: webmail site (cross-site). Target: `shop.example`.
2. `Strict` → cookie omitted on any cross-site request.
3. Server sees an anonymous request → login page or logged-out view.
4. This UX cost is why many sites use `Lax` for the main session cookie, sometimes plus a separate `Strict` cookie checked only for sensitive actions.

questions.prompt: The session cookie is set with `SameSite=Lax`. Which cross-site requests from `evil.example` to `app.example` will include it? Assume all other cookie conditions permit sending, the link and location examples navigate the top-level window, and no redirects intervene. Select all that apply.

options.text: An auto-submitted hidden `<form method="POST">`
options.explanation: Lax withholds cookies on cross-site POSTs. (The Lax+POST exception applies only to cookies with *no* SameSite attribute.)

options.text: The user clicking `<a href="https://app.example/x">`
options.explanation: Correct. A top-level navigation with a safe method gets `Lax` cookies.

options.text: ``
options.explanation: Images are subresource requests, not top-level navigations, so Lax cookies aren't sent.

options.text: `fetch("https://app.example/api", {credentials: "include"})`
options.explanation: A cross-site fetch is not a top-level navigation; Lax cookies are withheld even with `credentials: "include"`.

options.text: `window.location = "https://app.example/y"` (GET)
options.explanation: Correct. Script-initiated top-level GET navigation is still a top-level safe navigation, so Lax cookies go.

questions.workedExample:
Lax rule: send on cross-site requests **only** if top-level navigation **and** safe method.

| Request | Top-level? | Safe? | Sent |
|---|---|---|---|
| form POST | yes | no | no |
| link click | yes | yes | yes |
| img | no | yes | no |
| fetch | no | yes | no |
| location= | yes | yes | yes |

So Lax stops the classic POST CSRF but not unsafe GET endpoints.

questions.prompt: A site relies on Chromium's Lax-by-default behaviour instead of CSRF tokens. Its session cookie is set at login with **no** SameSite attribute. Thirty seconds after logging in, the user opens a malicious page that auto-submits a top-level cross-site POST form to `/transfer`. Assume a Chromium browser with the documented two-minute Lax+POST exception, and that all other cookie rules permit sending. What happens, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The cookie is withheld, because a missing SameSite is treated as Lax; no change is needed
options.explanation: This misses the Lax+POST exception for fresh cookies with no SameSite attribute. It also assumes every browser applies Lax by default; as of November 2026 only Chromium-based browsers do (Firefox and Safari do not).

options.text: The cookie is sent, because it is under two minutes old and has no explicit SameSite; set `SameSite=Lax` explicitly and keep a CSRF token (or equivalent) check
options.explanation: Correct. The exception applies only to cookies with no SameSite attribute, so explicit Lax removes it. A token check remains necessary for same-site attackers, unsafe GETs and browsers without Lax defaults.

options.text: The cookie is sent, because a missing SameSite means None; fix it with `SameSite=None; Secure`
options.explanation: Missing SameSite is not None in this configuration. And setting None would make things worse: the cookie would then go on every cross-site request that other rules permit.

options.text: Chromium blocks the cross-site form submission itself, so nothing needs fixing
options.explanation: SameSite never blocks requests; it only decides whether the cookie is attached. The form is always submitted.

questions.workedExample:
1. The cookie has no SameSite attribute, so Chromium applies its default mode, which is Lax-like.
2. Lax alone would withhold the cookie from a cross-site POST.
3. But the cookie is 30 seconds old, inside Chromium's two-minute Lax+POST window, and this is a top-level navigation, so the cookie is sent.
4. Fix in two parts: set `SameSite=Lax` explicitly (the exception never applies to explicit values), and keep CSRF tokens or an equivalent request check, because defaults differ between browsers and SameSite cannot stop same-site or client-side attacks.

Chromium describes the exception as temporary, so test the browsers you support rather than relying on it either way.

lessons.title: Request provenance, JSON types and framing
lessons.summary: Use request-context filters and strict API parsing alongside tokens, then block unwanted framing.
lessons.body:
Tokens check a secret; SameSite controls when cookies travel. This unit adds checks on where a request came from, closes a JSON-parsing gap, and then deals with clickjacking, which no request check can stop.

## Defence 3: checking where the request came from

Browsers add headers that a web page cannot set or change:

- **`Origin`** names the requesting page's origin on CORS requests and on every request whose method is not GET or HEAD, such as a form POST. Plain GET navigations and image loads usually carry none, and it can be `null` (opaque origins, some referrer policies). Accept only exact trusted origins, and decide deliberately what to do when it is absent.
- **`Sec-Fetch-Site`** (part of **Fetch Metadata**) says how the requesting page relates to your site: `same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site`, or `none` (the user typed the address or used a bookmark). Browsers send it only to HTTPS (and other trustworthy) URLs. OWASP notes that all major browsers have supported it since March 2023.

These headers describe a browser's request. `curl` or a script can send any values it likes, but such a client does not carry the victim's cookies, so this matters for CSRF only as a reminder that the headers are not authentication.

```python
SAFE = {"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"}

@app.before_request
def fetch_metadata():
    site = request.headers.get(
        "Sec-Fetch-Site")
    if site is None:
        return  # still require token
    if request.method in SAFE:
        return
    # Do not trust sibling sites by default.
    if site not in ("same-origin",
                    "none"):
        abort(403)
```

This hook rejects cross-site and same-site unsafe requests from supporting browsers, and does not treat sibling subdomains as trusted. When the header is missing (an old client, a stripping proxy), it falls back to the token check from earlier, which stays active.

OWASP's current guidance accepts a Fetch Metadata policy like this as a main defence for sites that only target modern browsers, *provided* missing headers fall back to origin checks or tokens. Keeping tokens as well costs little. Neither check stops same-origin XSS or client-side CSRF, because those requests really do come from your own page.

## JSON APIs

A common belief is "our API takes JSON, so it's immune". It depends:

- If the server *requires* `Content-Type: application/json`, a cross-site request with that type is not a simple request. It must pass a CORS preflight, and without permissive CORS the browser never sends it.
- If the server parses the body as JSON **regardless** of content type, an attacker can submit a form with `enctype="text/plain"`, crafted so that the body happens to be valid JSON. That is a simple request, sent with whatever cookies the browser's rules allow.

So: reject requests that are not `application/json`, or require a custom header such as `X-Requested-With`, which forces a preflight. Both rely on keeping CORS tight.

## Related: clickjacking

Instead of faking a request, the attacker loads your real page in an invisible iframe and tricks the user into clicking a button on it. Tokens don't help, because the click happens on your genuine page, which includes a valid token. Prevent the framing instead, with the `Content-Security-Policy` response header containing:

```
frame-ancestors 'none'
```

Use `'self'` if you frame your own pages, or list specific partner origins. `frame-ancestors` is a CSP directive, not a header of its own. `X-Frame-Options: DENY` is the older equivalent, still useful for old browsers. These stop framing-based clickjacking; they do not prevent every kind of deceptive interface.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a contract under a raffle ticket
> A con artist lays a real contract under a thin sheet printed with a raffle ticket, lining up "Sign here to win" with the contract's signature box. You think you are entering a raffle; your pen signs the contract.
>
> **How it maps:** The contract is your genuine page in a transparent iframe; the raffle sheet is the attacker's visible decoy page. The click is real, on your real button, with a valid token, which is why request checks cannot tell. `frame-ancestors` is a rule that your contract may never be placed under someone else's sheet.
>
> **Where it stops:** Nobody can stop a con artist layering paper, but a browser can refuse to render your page inside another site's frame. Some deceptive designs need no frame at all, and `frame-ancestors` does not cover those.

## Key takeaways
- Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site are browser-set filters; decide explicitly how to treat missing or `null` values, and fall back to tokens.
- A JSON API is protected only if it rejects non-JSON content types (or requires a custom header) and keeps CORS tight.
- `frame-ancestors` (or `X-Frame-Options`) prevents framing; tokens cannot stop a genuine framed click.

options.text: Reject it under the stated policy: same-site is not the allowed same-origin or none value

options.explanation: Supporting browsers can report same-site for cross-origin same-site contexts. Missing headers can reflect client or context differences, not just age; redirect history can also affect which value is reported.

options.text: Allow it, but only if the method is POST
options.explanation: POST is the dangerous case. The method doesn't change whether the initiator is trusted.

2. The policy accepts only `same-origin` and `none`.
3. `same-site` → 403.
4. Why it matters: if `blog.example.com` is taken over, SameSite cookies still flow (same site). Fetch Metadata can tell the difference; SameSite can't.

- Reject anything not `application/json`.
- Require a custom header with a restrictive CORS policy (requires preflight permission, which may be cached).

```
